text: One of the generally agreed upon features of morality is that it involves actions perceived to be binding on people. <break time="0.8s" /> This is the ought or should quality of morality that is the subject of a variety of types of philosophical analyses. <break time="0.8s" /> Many moral philosophers have been concerned with ways of characterizing procedures, judgments, and reasoning that lead to a sense of obligation. <break time="0.8s" /> In that case, judgments about obligations can be compatible with opposition and resistance to cultural practices and to the ways individuals are treated by society. <break time="0.8s" /> By contrast, in much of the field of psychology the sense of ought or obligation, not surprisingly, has been psychologized in the sense that there is a search for psychological mechanisms that produce changes involving accommodations to the values, norms, and practices of society. <break time="0.8s" /> Morality, then, is basically a form of compliance that becomes part of the individual through the formation of, as examples, habits, conscience, or traits of character. <break time="0.8s" /> In that context, opposition and resistance would be viewed as that which comes from the assertion of nonmoral or immoral individual drives, needs, interests, and desires.
